papers.title: GeoMER: A Joint Euclidean-Hyperbolic Geometry Framework for Multimodal Emotion Recognition
papers.abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) aims to understand human emotions by integrating information from multiple modalities such as speech and text. Psychological studies suggest that emotions exhibit latent hierarchical structured relationships in their semantic representations. However, most MER approaches rely on Euclidean representations, which capture fine-grained cross-modal interactions but do not explicitly provide a geometric prior for organizing hierarchical emotional structures. To mitigate this gap, we propose GeoMER, a joint Euclidean-Hyperbolic modeling framework that introduces hyperbolic emotion-core routing to capture higher-level, abstract emotional representations for MER. The proposed framework jointly models token-level cross-modal semantic interactions and latent emotion representations in two complementary geometric spaces. Specifically, GeoMER consists of a Euclide

papers.title: From Policy Evaluation to Off-Policy Control: Provable Emergence of In-Context Q-Learning
papers.abstract: Transformers can implement reinforcement-learning algorithms in context, yet how off-policy control emerges within Transformers remains poorly understood. We study Q-learning, a foundational model-free control algorithm that combines off-policy bootstrapping with greedy policy improvement. We prove that a two-layer attention-only Transformer can implement a finite-temperature form of Q-learning, where the temperature $τ>0$ controls the approximation to greedy action selection, recovering window Q-learning as $τ\to0$. We train the structured Transformer on randomly generated MDP tasks using output-only supervision. Experiments show that the theoretically predicted parameter structure emerges during training, including the internal greedy action-selection mechanism, and that the trained Transformer achieves performance comparable to Q-learning on unseen tasks. papers.title: Task-evoked eye movements as candidate digital biomarkers of depression severity in adolescents and young adults
papers.abstract: Objective digital measures of depression severity could complement conventional symptom assessments and facilitate more timely clinical evaluation. Here, we investigated whether task-evoked eye movements provide interpretable behavioral markers of depression severity in adolescents and young adults. In this single-center, cross-sectional study, 155 participants aged 14--20 years completed emotional-spatial free-viewing and memory-guided recall tasks and were stratified by 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores. We examined 19 prespecified eye-movement features across six task-informed domains using covariate-adjusted ordinal-trend models. papers.title: Graph-free Retrieval with Graph-Modified Embeddings
papers.abstract: Dense vector retrieval can miss evidence connected through intermediate entities, while direct graph retrieval requires access to the graph at query time. We compare five offline graph-based embedding transformations and strategies for using the resulting graph-modified embeddings alongside the originals, without query-time graph access. On a synthetic professional-network benchmark with complete supporting-evidence sets, direct replacement of the original embeddings reduces evidence recovery. Multi-stage strategies improve recovery by using graph-modified embeddings to guide the search while retaining the originals for semantic relevance. On questions requiring linked facts or comparisons among candidates, the strongest configuration improves recovery by up to 25.9% relative to plain vector retrieval. papers.title: Reset Early, Reset Often, Eliminate Models
papers.abstract: Connection-tableau provers typically construct closed tableaux by backtracking search. This gives lightweight proof procedures, but their low-memory search state leaves little derived information to reuse after a failed attempt. SATCoP addresses this by retaining grounded tableau clauses in an incremental SAT solver, allowing the prover to refute the problem once the accumulated ground clauses become propositionally unsatisfiable. We introduce SATResetCoP, which relies more directly on this persistent SAT state by not backtracking on unproductive tableaux and instead starting new ones to generate further ground clauses for the SAT solver. On TPTP, SATResetCoP improves over our leanCoP-style baseline by 54% and our SATCoP-style baseline by 18%. papers.title: Scaling Vision Transformers Without Training: Prune-and-Merge Token Compression
papers.abstract: Vision Transformers achieve strong performance but incur high computational costs from quadratic token interactions. Training-free token reduction methods improve efficiency, but their robustness remains underexplored. We propose Prune-and Merge ViT, a training-free framework for off-the-shelf models. It combines class attention-based pruning with similarity-based merging to reduce redundancy while preserving semantic information. To evaluate robustness we introduce two metrics. Relative Accuracy Drop (RAD) measures relative accuracy degradation under transformations, and Prediction Flip Rate (PFR) quantifies prediction consistency. On pretrained ViT and DeiT, Prune-and-Merge reduces computation competitively while maintaining robustness and better accuracy than existing token reduction methods. Our analysis suggests that hybrid token reduction does not introduce hallucination-like behav

papers.title: FASHION-RQ: Mining Hierarchical Semantic Structure for Automated Evaluation of Fashion Retrieval
papers.abstract: Evaluating fashion retrieval systems remains challenging due to the limited availability of benchmarks that capture the fine-grained, open-ended queries encountered in real-world search and recommendation. Existing benchmarks often rely on manual curation, predefined taxonomies, or synthetic prompts, limiting scalability and semantic coverage. We introduce FASHION-RQ: Mining Hierarchical Semantic Structure for Automated Evaluation of Fashion Retrieval, an automated framework that derives user-type queries and relevance sets directly from catalog structure. Our key insight is that hierarchical discrete representations learned by Residual Quantized Variational Autoencoders (RQ-VAE) organize products into semantically coherent clusters at progressively finer granularities. We leverage this structure to construct FASHION-RQBENCH, a scalable benchmark without manual query annotation or predef

papers.title: FALLNEST: Dual-Domain Dataset Condensation of Imbalanced IMU Data for Wearable Fall Detection
papers.abstract: Wearable fall detection is hampered by rare fall events, scarce labeled IMU data, and the cost of training deep models on large, imbalanced corpora. Existing methods either rely on hand-crafted features with shallow classifiers, which limits learning from raw signals, or train deep networks on full datasets that require re-sampling to counter class skew and demand substantial data and compute. To address this, we propose a novel Fall detection framework via Normalized-gradient and Embedding matched Synthetic Time-frequency condensation, dubbed FALLNEST, a data-centric approach that distills large, imbalanced IMU datasets into tiny, class-balanced synthetic training sets. Building on dual-domain time-series condensation (CondTSC), FALLNEST introduces a fall-specific 7-channel input with accelerometer vector magnitude, class-balanced K-Means initialization, and normalized gradient matching

papers.title: Uncertainty Evaluation: Bridging Machine Learning and Measurement Science
papers.abstract: Reliable uncertainty evaluation is essential for assessing the trustworthiness of machine learning (ML) predictions, particularly in safety-critical applications. This paper explores conceptual analogies between uncertainty evaluation in ML and measurement science, drawing on the evolution of metrology from error-based approaches to the framework established by the Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement (GUM). Particular attention is devoted to the distinction between process-level and result-level quality and to the limitations of the conventional classification of ML uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic components. It is argued that this dichotomy, similarly to the traditional distinction between random and systematic measurement errors, is inherently model-dependent and provides an insufficient basis for a unified uncertainty evaluation framework. papers.title: What Is the "Self" of a Large Language Model?
papers.abstract: What could the "self" of a large language model be, if it is neither a particular word nor a single privileged layer? We propose a relational account: a functional self is an actor-centered organization of information that distinguishes the model's recorded actions from externally supplied material while content and reasoning operations change. Its representational candidate is a family of layer-specific source-binding components, rather than one unchanged vector throughout the network. Preliminary observations from a 27B BF16 model provide a geometric starting point. papers.title: Code-Switching Detection via Language-Selective Dimensions in Speech Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Code-switching (CS), the alternation between languages within an utterance, is common in multilingual speech but underrepresented in pretraining corpora. Increasing CS coverage requires finding relevant utterances in large speech collections so that they can be included in training data. One way to find such utterances is to transcribe the speech and detect language alternation in the text, but this depends on obtaining accurate multilingual transcriptions. We propose a lightweight method that detects CS directly from speech. It uses frame-level language information in pretrained speech encoders to determine whether both languages are present within an utterance. Specifically, we identify language-selective hidden-state dimensions using monolingual recordings and aggregate their frame-level activations into a CS prediction. papers.title: Label Collapse in Diffusion Language Model In-Context Learning
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) applies large language models to new tasks by prepending a few labeled demonstrations to a query. Prior work has studied how demonstration ordering affects ICL, but the interaction between label arrangement patterns and model biases has not been systematically examined. We define label collapse as the failure mode in which the model generates query-independent labels, and show that it is architecturally universal at the tested 8-9B scale: five models spanning autoregressive (Llama-3, Qwen3.5) and discrete diffusion (LLaDA, iLLaDA, LLaDA-Instruct) families all exhibit label collapse even under the class-balanced alternating arrangement, with some label word pairs collapsing in virtually every tested condition and others flipping their collapse direction with arrangement. papers.title: Connecting the Dots: Enduring Performance Gaps in ASR Systems Between Standard and Minority English Varieties
papers.abstract: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) system evaluations have consistently revealed performance disparities along lines of race, gender, socioeconomic status, and language variety. While these disparities are well-documented, they are often (implicitly or explicitly) treated as issues that subsequent, larger, and more universal models will correct. We challenge this assumption of steady progress in reducing accent-related performance disparities, conducting a longitudinal evaluation of 16 prominent systems released between 2021-2025 across 8 datasets representing diverse English accent varieties. We find that the performance disparity between Mainstream US English (MUSE) and minority accents is stubborn, not reliably declining as a function of time. papers.title: Gluing Local Contexts into Global Meaning: A Sheaf-Theoretic Decomposition of Transformer Representations
papers.abstract: Existing interpretability tools do not test whether a representation keeps the same content when only the phrasing changes. We treat each paraphrase pair as a local witness that two activations should agree and build a cellular sheaf over the paraphrase graph; its Laplacian $L_\mathcal{F}$ answers the question on a frozen model with no training. The kernel $H^0$ is a content subspace: at 20 dimensions it beats the preserved subspace of the concept eraser LEACE on held-out CounterFact fact retrieval across eight architectures by a mean $+17.1$\,pp, and constraining all paraphrases of a fact jointly adds a further $+6.5$\,pp. The spectral complement concentrates causal influence: ablating the most paraphrase-variable coordinates, a coordinate-wise proxy for it, changes model outputs $5.6$ to $26.5\times$ more than ablating coordinates of matched per-coordinate variability, across nine mode

papers.title: A Benchmark for Bangla Task-Oriented Dialogue Understanding
papers.abstract: Task-oriented dialogue understanding remains underexplored for Bangla, particularly in multilingual settings involving English and romanized Bangla (Banglish). We introduce BanglaTOD, a parallel tri-lingual benchmark comprising 209 multi-turn dialogues across nine Bangladesh-specific service domains and 64 intents. Each conversational turn is aligned across Bangla, English, and Banglish, yielding 4,689 language-specific turn records annotated with intents, token-level slots, state updates, and accumulated dialogue states. We establish context-aware baselines for joint intent classification and slot filling using mBERT, BERT-base-uncased, and BanglaBERT. Cross-language analysis reveals substantial performance differences across models and linguistic representations, while removing dialogue history reduces intent accuracy by 19.0--25.7 percentage points. papers.title: Geometric Structure Predicts Per-Example Neighborhood Loss Under PCA Truncation
papers.abstract: Dimensionality reduction can preserve the average performance of text embeddings even when a substantial fraction of their dimensions is removed. Aggregate metrics, however, do not reveal whether degradation is distributed uniformly across examples. We study per-example neighborhood stability under PCA truncation across static word embeddings and modern sentence encoders. Per-item neighbor retention varies widely and is predictable from geometric properties of the representation and its alignment with the retained PCA subspace. papers.title: Swiss4Arg: A Parallel Dataset for Multilingual Argument Mining across Swiss National Languages
papers.abstract: We present Swiss4Arg, a multilingual dataset for argument mining based on official Swiss voting brochures, covering all four national languages: German, French, Italian, and Romansh (a Romance minority language exclusively spoken in Switzerland). The brochures contain explicitly formulated arguments systematically organized into pro and con sections, resulting in a cross-lingually aligned resource with balanced argumentative stance. We create a dataset that comprises 53 federal voting issues collected between 2019 and 2025, annotated for argument components (major claims, claims, premises, and non-argumentative units) and relations (support and attack) by three native speakers per language. papers.title: RegExtract: A Benchmark for PFAS Regulatory Information Extraction with LLMs
papers.abstract: Extracting structured information from regulatory documents is a critical but challenging task. Relevant facts are scattered across long, legally dense texts, and traceability of extracted facts to their source is essential for verification. With increasing awareness of the environmental and health impacts of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), regulatory documents have expanded significantly, varying in scope and product relevance, making interpretation challenging for manufacturers and policymakers. We introduce RegExtract, a benchmark for structured information extraction from PFAS regulatory documents, comprising 488 human-annotated field instances across 20 US state documents and 46 regulations. Each field instance includes a value and a provenance entry, yielding 976 entries in total. We define a typed, multi-field schema targeting key elements such as material definitions,

papers.title: Do LLMs differentiate linguistic traits internally?: A layer-wise analysis
papers.abstract: Large language models often produce judgments that resemble human responses, but it remains unclear whether they internally capture linguistic nuances such as conventional versus idiomatic meaning. A layer-wise representational analysis was conducted on two equal-sized pre-trained models, Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma-3-1B-PT, to examine whether and where these models differentiate linguistic traits from input. The analysis combined layer-wise probing with geometric distance measures, using the top embedding dimensions ranked by principal component loadings for each layer. papers.title: Scale, Drivers, and Limits of Representational Alignment Across Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Comparing large language models can reveal shared representational structure and systematic differences between them. However, aggregate similarity measures can obscure how agreement varies across geometric scales and which linguistic properties support it. We introduce two complementary methods to resolve where models agree and what supports that agreement. Standard representational similarity analysis (RSA) summarizes similarity across all stimulus pairs, potentially obscuring differences in alignment between nearby and distant inputs. Neighborhood-Weighted RSA (NW-RSA) addresses this limitation by weighting stimulus pairs according to their proximity in representational space, placing alignment from local neighborhoods to global geometry on a common scale. papers.title: PatTransBench: an ipc-stratified, multi-dimensional benchmark for patent machine translation evaluation
papers.abstract: We present PatTransBench, a 12,000-item Chinese-English/Japanese/Korean patent machine translation (PatMT) benchmark with a four-dimensional evaluation protocol. The benchmark comprises 6,000 short-text (sentence/claim) and 6,000 long-text (paragraph) pairs, evenly split across three language pairs and both translation directions, built via IPC-section-stratified sampling and dualthreshold quality gating from upstream patent-family parallel corpora. The evaluation protocol spans literal n-gram overlap (BLEU, ROUGE-L, chrF), cross-lingual semantic textual similarity (CLSTS), 38-probe-language consistency testing, and serving performance under concurrency. papers.title: Intent-Triggered Anchoring for Multi-Token Format Units in Parallel Decoding of Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: In parallel decoding, diffusion language models commit several tokens per forward pass, so co-committed tokens cannot see each other, breaking multi-token format units that parsers need. On ECHO, an open-weight one-step chest X-ray (CXR) report generator, 32.7-36.7% of evaluation reports lack a parseable Impression heading and score as empty. We propose intent-triggered anchoring, a training-free decoding rule that completes a format unit once the model commits its first token, inserting only units with a unique, content-free completion; fallbacks write the unit when the model stops or loops without starting it. On three CXR evaluation sets, the rule raises readable rates from 63.3-67.3% to 100.0% with no regressions and a 95th-percentile latency ratio of 0.68-1.28 against official decoding. papers.title: Learning Proposition-Level Links from Sentence-Level Supervision for Neuro-Symbolic NLI
papers.abstract: We study neuro-symbolic natural language inference (NLI) with independently translated propositional representations of the premise and hypothesis. Before symbolic reasoning, the system must infer semantic links between their proposition-level units (atoms). Existing systems based on Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) and Boolean satisfiability (SAT) identify these links using fixed embedding-based source selection and pretrained sentence-level NLI models not trained for atom-level linking. We introduce a trainable atom linker that jointly predicts link existence, source selection, and relation type. Without atom-pair training annotations, we treat cross-formula link structures as latent and train the linker from sentence-level NLI labels, keeping the translator and SAT reasoner fixed. papers.title: Towards Autopilot Labeling for Short Video Content Governance
papers.abstract: The explosive growth of short videos has presented significant challenges to content governance. Traditional manual labeling is inefficient, slow to iterate, and costly. Therefore, we explore and develop a multi-stage autopilot labeling framework aimed at progressively increasing the level of automation in short video content annotation. To move beyond the heavy reliance on human expert labeling at the initial L0 stage, we first introduce a discriminative MLLM labeler at the L1 stage, which is fine-tuned with supervised data to directly predict labels for short videos. Advancing to the L2 stage, we shift to a domain-adaptive MLLM pretrained on short video data and use it for zero-shot labeling, enabling flexible generalization without task-specific supervision. papers.title: Who Receives Respect? A Counterfactual Benchmark for Honorific Allocation Bias in Bengali
papers.abstract: Bengali has no grammatical gender, but honorificity is obligatory: every third-person reference must choose ordinary or respectful register. English has no such signal, so the system must choose a level of deference that the source never specified. We use this property to measure how large language models (LLMs) allocate respect in English--Bengali translation. Our evaluation set contains 2{,}016 sentences across 72 occupations. Each appears in seven sentence frames under four pronoun conditions. Masculine and feminine versions differ by one word, forming counterfactual pairs. We report a single Honorific Bias Score (HBS) for each model on a 0--100 scale, covering both the gender and occupation axes. A lower score means that respect is allocated more evenly. papers.title: Amharic-English Cross-Language Question Answering Using Statistical Machine Translation, Named Entity Recognition, and Semantic Indexing
papers.abstract: The predominance of English-language Web content creates an information-access barrier for speakers of low-resource languages such as Amharic. This paper presents the design, imple-mentation, and evaluation of a bidirectional Amharic-English cross-language question answering (CLQA) system that allows a user to formulate a natural-language question in either Amharic or English and retrieve an answer from documents written in the other language. The system integrates a statistical machine translation (SMT) component for query translation, a maximum-entropy named entity recognition (NER) component for Amharic text processing, semantic-based indexing, question analysis, passage retrieval, and answer extraction. papers.title: Natural Language Processing for Aligning Readings with Learning Objectives and Assessing Topic Balance in Dental Education
papers.abstract: Curriculum teams often lack time to check whether assigned readings support learning objectives (LOs) and whether topic coverage is balanced. We present a natural language processing (NLP) workflow to support evidence-informed curation of reading lists. The workflow combines PubMedBERT sentence embeddings and cosine similarity for retrieval, natural language inference (NLI) for evidence checking, and topic modeling for coverage analysis. We tested the approach in dental education using 13 course-level LOs and a PubMed-derived corpus of 3,837 LO-abstract pairs. Median cosine similarity ranged from 0.86 to 0.91 across the 13 LOs, showing generally high semantic similarity. Topic modeling showed broad but uneven coverage, with one or two dominant topics per domain. papers.title: Robust Marathi Sentiment Analysis using Domain-Adaptive Pre-training and Data Augmentation Approaches
papers.abstract: For languages with limited resources, Sentiment Analysis remains a challenging problem due to limited annotated data and strong domain variability across textual sources. Marathi, despite being widely spoken, lacks extensive multi-domain sentiment analysis studies. Recent efforts by L3Cube have introduced multi-domain datasets in Marathi, enabling a better study of domain-aware sentiment classification. This study uses the pretrained MahaBERT model to improve sentiment classification for Marathi across different domains. Models are trained on individual domain datasets and domain-adaptive pretraining is applied using masked language modeling to help the model better understand domain-specific language. papers.title: REPRO: Reflective Evolutionary Prompt Optimizer for Automated LLM Red-Teaming
papers.abstract: Safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to adversarial prompts that bypass their safety training. Existing automated red-teaming methods either require privileged access unavailable in production, rely on manually engineered per-model templates, or optimize a single objective without population-level diversity. We present REPRO (Reflective Evolutionary Prompt Optimization), a pure black-box framework that discovers adversarial prompts through evolutionary optimization driven entirely by a compressed open-weight 7B reflective model on a single consumer GPU. REPRO introduces two mechanisms absent from prior work, both isolated in a component ablation: semantic crossover, an LLM-guided multi-parent recombination operator, and Bayesian strategy selection via Thompson Sampling informed by structured failure analysis. papers.title: Sanzaru: Benchmarking Protocol Formation under Epistemic & Communication Asymmetry
papers.abstract: A language model's ability to solve a task individually does not ensure that a team can solve it under unequal access to information and communication. SANZARU examines this gap through cooperative bomb-defusal puzzles adapted from BOMBANANA! (Lefto Studio, 2026). Task information and action authority are divided among three agents: one cannot hear, another cannot speak, and the third cannot see. The benchmark contains 120 puzzle instances across seven families, each targeting a distinct coordination ability. Across 1512 episodes, 7 models achieve an overall success rate of 49%, ranging from 20% to 86% under the evaluated configurations. Teams develop or adopt diverse communication protocols, from simple gesture codes to Morse and encodings of entire manuals. papers.title: The Constitution Speaks Nheengatu: An Open MT System and Reproducible Corpus Pipeline for the Amazonian Língua Geral
papers.abstract: Nheengatu (yrl), the Amazonian Língua Geral, has 6--10 thousand speakers and is co-official in São Gabriel da Cachoeira (Brazil), yet remains poorly served by evaluated Portuguese--Nheengatu MT resources. We present the largest parallel corpus assembled for the language (14.5k Portuguese--Nheengatu pairs), anchored by the 2023 official translation of the Brazilian Federal Constitution; the first MT evaluation set built from transcribed spontaneous speech; and, to our knowledge, the first open-weight MT models dedicated to bidirectional Portuguese--Nheengatu translation. Three findings organize the paper. First, translation into Nheengatu on held-out constitutional articles plateaus on development data regardless of training length or model size, and much of the remaining error sits in conventional legal terms that the written sources do not attest consistently; a terminology success rate

papers.title: Omni-Modal LLMs Know More Than They Say
papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) extend LLMs to process heterogeneous modalities (e.g., vision, audio, and IMU signals) alongside language, enabling a broader range of multimodal tasks. Yet we find that these models often fail to express information from non-textual modalities even when they perceive it correctly. We term this disconnect knows-but-cannot-say. To investigate this phenomenon, we introduce Token-level Modality Alignment (TMA), which measures the alignment between individual modality representations and response representations. Our analysis shows that non-textual representations are less aligned with response tokens and receive less attention than textual representations, suggesting a potential explanation for uneven modality preferences. papers.title: Review Rarely Beats the Stronger Model: Separating Verification from Capability Transfer in LLM Pipelines
papers.abstract: Qwen3-8B reviewing Llama-3.1-8B in math adds 33.2 points, yet Qwen3-8B alone is 6.4 points more accurate than the result. Reviewing another model's answer is usually judged by its gain over the generator. We show that this confuses verification, which adds accuracy beyond either model alone, with capability transfer, where a stronger reviewer supplies answers it could have given on its own. Measured against the stronger model alone, across 48 pairs of 12 open-weight models (3B to 72B) in math, knowledge, code and reasoning, review beats it in only 9 of 96 review directions, and does worse the larger the capability gap. The reason is that the reviewer mostly follows the generator, discarding its own correct answers. papers.title: PAT: A Personality-Driven Augmentation and Transfer Learning Framework for Depression Detection on Social Media
papers.abstract: Depression is a prevalent mental disorder that affects millions worldwide, with early detection crucial for effective intervention. While exist?ing methods have achieved promising results in automated depression detection, they face two key limitations: (1) noise in post screening: symptom-based semantic screening is easily misled by superficial lexical patterns, thereby introducing false-positive posts; (2) weak op?timization of the post encoder: relying solely on coarse user-level supervision signals pre?vents models from capturing depressive cues within individual posts. To address these limita?tions, we propose PAT, a Personality-driven Augmentation and Transfer learning frame?work. papers.title: Do LLM Tutors Actually Teach? A Process-Centered Synthesis of the Tutoring Loop
papers.abstract: Large language models can produce fluent tu- toring dialogue, but whether they actually help students learn remains unclear. We present a process-centered synthesis of LLM tutoring that follows the path from learner-state infer- ence to pedagogical action, tutor training, eval- uation, and student simulation. This view ex- poses a central gap: implementing a tutoring component does not establish that it works or that its outputs meaningfully affect later stages. A structured study-level audit shows that peda- gogical evaluation is common, while evidence becomes much thinner for learner-conditioned intervention, human learning gains, and espe- cially transfer or delayed retention. Human studies nevertheless provide a conditional posi- tive result: LLM tutors can improve learning, but benefits depend on pedagogical structure, learner engagement, and how learning is mea- sured. papers.title: Latent Taxonomies: How Property Induction Develops in Language Model Pre-training
papers.abstract: When told that robins have sesamoid bones, people are far more prone to extend the property to sparrows than to whales. This behavior, called category-based property induction, is well documented in humans, but whether and how it develops in language models trained only to predict the next token is unclear. To shed light on this, we construct a hierarchical taxonomy of synthetic entities grouped by the properties they share. We then inject facts from this latent taxonomy into the continued pre-training of Pythia and OLMo 2 models from 70M to 7B parameters, and track the development of inductive behaviors. We find that taxonomically aligned induction emerges from next-token prediction alone: a property learned for one entity transfers more strongly within its taxonomic category than across categories. papers.title: From Candidate Tokens to Final Outcomes: Decoding Relative Long-Horizon Candidate Value from Reasoning Model Representations
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models generate reasoning trajectories token by token. At a given prefix, multiple next-token candidates may be plausible, yet shape subsequent reasoning and differ in their chances of leading to the correct answer. Whether these differences are reflected in internal representations remains unclear. To study this question, we define relative long-horizon candidate value to quantify within-prefix differences and construct the Reasoning Candidate-Token Value (RCTV) dataset, pairing mathematical reasoning prefixes with plausible next-token candidates and their empirical long-horizon candidate values. Using RCTV, we examine hidden states, multilayer perceptron outputs, and attention outputs at candidate positions with sparse linear probes.
